subject: Computing

unit.unitOverview:
Welcome to Unit 1 of Year 8. This is a big, exciting unit, and it is the heart of everything you will do in computing this year. You are going to learn how to think like a programmer and then how to write real programs in Python, one of the most popular programming languages in the world. You will design algorithms on paper, turn them into working code on a computer, and even send messages wirelessly between tiny physical computers called micro:bits.

Last year, in Year 7, you met flowcharts, block-based coding and the very first ideas of Python. This year you move up a level. You will write pseudocode to plan programs, use selection to make programs decide things, follow searching algorithms, write conditional statements in text-based Python, handle different kinds of data, borrow ready-made code from libraries, learn the professional habits of software development, and finish with hands-on physical computing. That is the whole journey from an idea in your head to a program running on a real device.

This is a self-paced unit, so you move at your own speed. Your AI tutor is available 24 hours a day to explain an idea another way, quiz you, or help you find a bug. Everything here uses free, open-source software: you will write Python in a friendly editor called Thonny, which you can download for free from thonny.org, and you will program micro:bits in your web browser at python.microbit.org - with no hardware needed, because it has a built-in simulator.

concepts.title: Pseudocode
concepts.explanation:
Pseudocode is a tool used when *designing* a program, before you write the real code. The word is made of two parts: *pseudo* means 'not real', and *code* means programming statements. So pseudocode means 'not-real code'. It looks like a program, but it does not have to follow the strict rules of any one language. Think of it as a bridge: on one side is a flowchart or plain English, and on the other side is a high-level programming language like Python. Pseudocode sits halfway between them.

Why bother with something 'not real'? Because a plan lets you think clearly. When you write pseudocode you can work out what the program should do - the variables you need and the calculations you must perform - without worrying about getting every colon, bracket and spelling exactly right. It is like planning an essay: you jot down your main points first, and worry about perfect spelling and grammar later.

Pseudocode is also language independent. That means a programmer who uses Python, and another who uses a different language, can both read the same pseudocode and then build it in their own language. This matters because large programs are written by many people. A shared plan lets the whole team understand each other. There is no single fixed syntax for pseudocode - INPUT, Input and input could all be used - but you should stay consistent within one program, or it gets confusing.

Every program is built from three programming constructs, and pseudocode can show all three:

Sequence - the order that statements run in, from top to bottom.

Selection - checking a condition and running different code depending on whether it is true or false (this is Subunit 1.2).

Iteration - repeating code in a loop (you will use this in later units).

An input statement tells the program that the user needs to enter a value, and it needs a variable to store that value in. We will use the keyword INPUT:

Pseudocode: three input statements

An output statement sends data out, usually to the screen. We will use the keyword OUTPUT. Any text you want to show exactly must go inside double quotation marks. Without the quotation marks, the word would be treated as a variable name instead:

Pseudocode: outputting a fixed message

To join pieces of text together we use concatenation. In this pseudocode we join with a comma, although a plus sign or an ampersand can also be used. Here the program greets the user by name:

Pseudocode: if the user enters Nadia, the output is 'Hello, Nadia'

A variable is a named location in memory that stores one item of data, and that data can change as the program runs. Storing data in a variable is called assignment. In our pseudocode we use an arrow to mean 'assign', because the equals sign can be confused with the 'is equal to' test used in conditions. The left-hand side is the variable's identifier (its name), then the arrow, then the data to store:

Pseudocode: storing 'Red' in colour and 12 in age

An identifier must be one word with no spaces, must not start with a number or symbol, must not be a reserved keyword, and should be unique within the program. Reserved keywords are special words the language already uses. In Python 3 there are 35 reserved keywords, such as if, else, for, while, def, import, True and False. A helpful correction to a common mistake: in Python 3, print is not a keyword - it is a built-in function - so you technically could name a variable print, but you never should, because it would hide the useful function.

Arithmetic operators are symbols for calculations. In computing we write multiply as * and divide as / (not the maths signs). The four you need are + (add), - (subtract), * (multiply) and / (divide). Each operator needs a number (or a variable holding a number) on both sides, and the result should be stored or output. Here is a worked example that adds two numbers:

Pseudocode: stores 1 and 2, adds them, outputs 3

You can also output a calculation directly without storing it first:

To follow or trace an algorithm, start at the first line and do exactly what each line says, in order, one line at a time. Do not jump ahead. A useful trick is to cover the algorithm with a piece of paper and slide it down to reveal one line at a time. Write down the value held in each variable, and cross out the old value whenever it changes. Trace this shopping-total example, which Nadia could use at the family stall:

Pseudocode: adds three costs onto a running total

With the inputs 10, 20, 10 and 25 entered in order, total starts as 10, then becomes 30, then 40, then 65, so the output is 'The total cost is 65'. Notice how the same variable total is updated again and again - that is the point of a variable.
concepts.example: Pseudocode has been used since the earliest days of computing to share program ideas between people who used completely different machines and languages. Because it belongs to no single language, it never goes out of date.

concepts.title: Selection in Pseudocode
concepts.explanation:
Selection is how a program makes a decision. It checks a condition - a comparison that is either true or false - and runs different code depending on the answer. The comparison operators are:

A conditional statement (often called an IF statement) has three parts: a condition that can be true or false, some statements that run when it is true, and (sometimes) some statements that run when it is false.
concepts.example: The simplest form is IF THEN. Code between THEN and ENDIF runs only when the condition is true. The code inside is indented (moved to the right) so it is easy to see. If the condition is false, that code is skipped:

concepts.title: Pseudocode: ELSEIF chain with a final ELSE
concepts.explanation:
Important rule: once one condition is found to be true, its code runs and the rest of the chain is skipped. So if the user enters '1234', the first condition is false, the second is true, '1234 is not a strong password' is output, and nothing else in the chain is checked.

Boolean operators: AND, OR, NOT

Boolean operators let one condition combine or reverse others. *Boolean* means a value that can only be true or false. Their rules are:

AND needs a condition on each side. The result is true only when both are true.

OR needs a condition on each side. The result is true when at least one is true; it is false only when both are false.

NOT takes one condition and reverses it: true becomes false, and false becomes true.
concepts.example: To work out a combined condition, replace each simple condition with its result, then apply the operator. In this AND example, total is 97:

concepts.title: Pseudocode: AND combines two conditions
concepts.explanation:
Condition 1, 97 > 90, is true. Condition 2, 97 < 100, is true. True AND true is true, so 'Just in range' is output. If total were 100 instead, then 100 < 100 is false, and true AND false is false, so the ELSE would run and output 'Incorrect amount'.

For NOT, look at this example where quantity is 0:

Pseudocode: NOT reverses the condition

The condition quantity = 0 is true, and NOT true is false, so the ELSE runs: 'No items remaining'.
concepts.example: When you mix Boolean operators, they run in a set order (their precedence), just like BIDMAS in maths. NOT runs first, then AND, then OR. Brackets change the order: whatever is inside brackets runs first. You will not have to read very complicated conditions, but you must understand that brackets group conditions together and make your meaning clear. When in doubt, add brackets.

concepts.title: Searching Algorithms
concepts.explanation:
A searching algorithm is a set of steps for finding a particular item in a set of data. Computers search constantly. When you log in, the system searches a file of usernames to find yours and then checks the password. When you look for a lost file, the computer searches every file for a match. When you use a search engine, it searches web pages for your keywords. Searching well saves huge amounts of time.

There are many searching algorithms, and the best one depends on the situation. Some are faster when there is a very large amount of data; others only work when the data is already in order. There is no single algorithm that is always best. The simplest and most important one to learn first is the linear search.

*Linear* means 'in a straight line'. A linear search looks at the first item, then the second, then the third, and so on, in order, until it either finds what it is looking for or reaches the end. Think of turning face-down cards one at a time, from left to right, checking each. The steps are:

Compare it with the value you are searching for.

If it matches, stop - you have found it.

If it does not match, move to the next item.

Repeat from step 2 until you find the value, or there are no items left.

If you run out of items, the value is not there.

For Ehel Academy's library book finder, imagine the titles are in this order: 'cat', 'rabbit', 'mouse', 'sheep', 'horse'. To find 'horse', a linear search checks 'cat' (no), 'rabbit' (no), 'mouse' (no), 'sheep' (no), 'horse' (yes - found at the fifth item). If you searched for 'lion', it would check all five, find no match, and report that 'lion' is not in the list.

You plan and trace searches on paper first, then you can build them in Python. Here a list holds the numbers, a while loop moves through them one at a time, and a flag called found records success. (Positions in a Python list start counting at 0.)

Python: a linear search using a while loop and a found flag

This program checks 20, 1, 13, 66, 78, then reaches 33 at position 5, sets found to True, stops the loop, and outputs 'Found 33 at position 5'. If you change target to 99, the loop checks every number, never sets found, and outputs '99 is not in the list'. You will run and modify this in your Activities booklet.
concepts.example: Search engines guard their searching algorithms like treasure. A search engine that finds the most useful results the fastest attracts the most users, so companies spend years improving how they search. When you research online, always use safe, trusted websites, and ask your teacher if you are unsure.

concepts.title: Conditional Statements in Text-Based Programming (Python)
concepts.explanation:
Now you turn your pseudocode into real Python and run it in Thonny. A conditional statement in Python is an if statement, and Python also has else and elif. They work just like IF, ELSE and ELSEIF in pseudocode, but the syntax is exact and you must get it right.

The if statement and indentation

An if statement is written with the lowercase word if, then the condition, then a colon :. The code that runs when the condition is true goes on the next line and must be indented (usually four spaces). Python has no ENDIF; instead, the indentation itself shows which lines are inside the if. When you type the colon and press Enter, Thonny usually indents for you.

Python: prints the message only if the user types purple

colour = input("What colour is made when red and blue are mixed? ")

Notice == with two equals signs. In Python, = means 'assign a value', while == means 'is equal to'. Mixing them up is one of the most common beginner errors. The comparison operators in Python are >, <, >=, <=, == (equal to) and != (not equal to).

Here is a pass check. int() turns the typed text into a whole number so it can be compared:

Python: prints 'You passed' when the score is 50 or more

else runs when the condition is false. It is written in lowercase, has no condition, and is followed by a colon. The if and the else line up at the same indentation:

colour = input("What colour is made when red and blue are mixed? ")

For more than two choices, use elif (short for 'else if'). Python checks each condition in order and runs the block for the first one that is true. Here is Ehel Academy's grade reporter as Python:

Python: elif chain with a final else

If the user enters 72, then 72 >= 80 is false, 72 >= 60 is true, so 'Silver star' prints and the rest is skipped. The order matters: you test the highest boundary first.

Python is case sensitive: the letter H is not the same as h. So if answer == "yes": is true for 'yes' but false for 'Yes' or 'YES'. Programmers handle this with the Boolean operators.

Boolean operators in Python: and, or, not

concepts.title: Data in Text-Based Programs
concepts.explanation:
Computers need to know what type of data they are working with. You have met these data types:

The Boolean data type holds only one of two values: True or False - nothing else. In Python these are written with a capital first letter, True and False, and with no quotation marks. The quotation marks matter enormously: "True" (with quotes) is a *string* - the word 'True' - while True (no quotes) is the Boolean value. They behave completely differently.

Python: two Boolean values and one string

A flag is a Boolean variable used to record whether something has happened - true means it happened, false means it did not. It is like a flag raised at a football match to signal an event. Here the flag adult records whether the user is 18 or over:

A neat trick: because age >= 18 is already a true/false test, you can store its result directly. The next line does exactly the same job as the whole if...else above:

Python: a comparison stored straight into a Boolean flag

Later, you can use the flag in a condition without repeating the test. Also, because adult is already True or False, you can simply write if adult: instead of if adult == True: - both mean the same thing.

A constant is like a variable, but its value is not meant to change while the program runs. A good example is pi in maths - it is always about 3.14. Using a constant has three benefits: you will not accidentally change the value; if you ever need to update it, you change it in just one place; and a well-named constant makes your code easier to read.

Python does not have a built-in way to lock a constant without a special library, so by convention we write constant names in UPPERCASE to remind ourselves not to change them. Here 10 is stored in a constant TEN:

Python: using UPPERCASE to mark a constant

For Nadia's stall, the price-per-kilo and a repeated message are perfect constants:

Python: two constants used more than once

Casting means converting data from one type to another. You already use int(), float() and str(). There is also bool(), which converts a value to a Boolean. The rules can surprise you:

The big surprise is that bool("False") is True, because it is a non-empty *string*, not the Boolean False. This is why we never put quotation marks around a real Boolean. This little program uses casting to check whether the user typed anything at all:

Python: an empty entry casts to False; any word casts to True

Some programming languages store True and False as the binary values 1 and 0. That is because deep down, every value in a computer is just patterns of 1s and 0s, and a Boolean fits perfectly into a single bit.

Data type — Meaning · Examples · Cast · Result · Why

Integer — A whole number · 0, 34, 998 · bool(1) or bool(-23) · True · Any number that is not zero is True

Real (float) — A number with a decimal point · 0.0, 1.25, 33.5 · bool(0) · False · Zero is False

Character — A single letter, number or symbol · 'h', '9', '?' · bool("Hello") or bool("False") · True · ANY non-empty string is True - even the word 'False'

String — One or more characters treated as text · "hello", "001", "22 fils" · bool("") · False · An empty string is False

concepts.title: Library Programs
concepts.explanation:
Before libraries, you need sub-routines. A sub-routine is a self-contained, named block of code. You call it by its name, it runs its statements, then control returns to where you called it. There are two kinds: a function returns a value to the program that called it, while a procedure just does a job and returns nothing. In Python all sub-routines are written the same way with def, so at this stage you can call them all functions.

Defining and calling a function

You define a function with def, a name, brackets () and a colon. The code inside is indented. The keyword return sends a value back:

Python: a function that returns a string

When the program reaches print(greeting()), it calls greeting(), which returns 'Hello'. So the line acts like print("Hello"). The output is 'Hello' then 'This is my program'.

A parameter is a value you pass into a function, written inside the brackets when you call it. This function takes the length of a side and returns the area of a square:

Python: a function with a parameter and a return value

If the user enters 5, then square_area(5) returns 25, which is stored in area, so the output is 'The area is 25'. You do not need to know *how* a function works inside - only what to give it and what it gives back.

A program library is a collection of ready-made sub-routines that other programmers have already written and tested. Instead of writing common code yourself - like working out pi, or generating a random number - you import a library and use its functions. Libraries make programming faster, are usually well tested and reliable, and let you do things you might not know how to write from scratch. Using a library is not cheating: professional programmers rely on them every day.

Two cautions. First, still check the results are what you expect - test your program. Second, be careful which libraries you download, because anyone can publish one and a bad library could contain a virus. Stick to well-known libraries and trusted sources.

Some common Python libraries are:

To use a library, put import and its name at the top of your program. Then call a function with the library name, a dot, and the function name. The math library gives you floor (round down), ceil (round up) and pi:

Python: importing and using the math library

math.floor(22.6) returns 22 (rounded down). math.ceil(22.6) returns 23 (rounded up). math.pi returns 3.141592653589793. Notice math.pi has no brackets - it is a value, not a function you call with arguments. The return value is not saved unless you use it, so you can print() it or store it in a variable. For Ehel Academy's building project, here is the area of a circle:

Python: area of a circle using math.pi

A random number is chosen by chance, with no pattern. The random library's randint function returns a random whole number between two values you give as parameters - and both end values can be produced:

Python: a random whole number from 1 to 6, like rolling a dice

random.randint(1, 6) could return 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6. random.randint(100, 103) could return 100, 101, 102 or 103. This is perfect for Ehel Academy's quiz game, to pick which question to ask, or to decide which way a game character moves.

When this book was written there were over 137,000 Python libraries that people could import into their programs. That is a giant, free toolbox built and shared by programmers all over the world.

Library — What it provides

math — Mathematical values and functions, such as pi and rounding

random — Generating random numbers

pandas — Working with larger, structured sets of data

tensorflow — Artificial intelligence, such as machine learning

concepts.title: Software Development
concepts.explanation:
This subunit teaches the professional habits that turn a beginner into a real programmer: breaking problems down, building in small steps, predicting what code will do, and testing thoroughly.

Decomposition means breaking a large problem into smaller sub-problems. It is much easier to solve several small problems and combine the solutions than to tackle one giant problem. A sub-problem can still be broken into steps; a single step cannot be broken down any further. For example, designing an intruder alarm decomposes into three sub-problems: 'set the alarm', 'check for an intruder' and 'turn the alarm off'. Each of those then breaks into steps.

There is usually more than one correct way to decompose a problem. Decomposition helps because it is natural for humans (you would tidy a house room by room, not all at once), it lets many people work on different parts at the same time, it lets specialists focus on what they do best, and it often reveals repeating parts that can become reusable sub-routines. For Ehel Academy's quiz game you might decompose it into: show a question, get the answer, check the answer, keep the score, and show the final result.

Iterative development means building a program in small stages, testing each part before moving on. *Iterative* means repeating. Instead of writing the whole program and then testing it all at once, you write a little, test it, fix or add, test again, and repeat until it is finished. This is smart because a small piece of code has fewer places for a bug to hide, so problems are easier to find and fix. If you were writing a Fire, Water, Earth game, you might first get the two players' names working and test that, then add the choice of element and test that, and so on.

To predict an outcome is to say what you think a program will do *before* you run it. You read the code carefully, follow the logic, and write down the expected output for given inputs. Then you run the program (or trace the algorithm) to check whether you were right. Predicting is one of the best ways to deepen your understanding, which is why the activities keep asking you to predict first, then run.

Running a program once with one input does not prove it works. You must test it many times with different data. There are three kinds of test data:

Normal test data - sensible values that should be accepted, well inside the allowed range.

Invalid test data - values that should be rejected, outside the allowed range.

Boundary test data - values right on the edge of what is and is not allowed; these catch the most bugs.

Boundaries matter. Consider a program meant to let anyone aged 16 or under join a club:

Python: a program with a hidden bug

Test it with 10 (normal) and it works. Test it with 20 (invalid) and it works. But test the boundary, 16, and it fails: 16 < 16 is false, so a 16-year-old is wrongly refused. The condition should have been age <= 16. Only the boundary test revealed the bug. This is exactly why boundary testing is so important.

A test plan is a table that records your tests. A common layout has columns for the type of data, a description, the example input, the expected output, and the actual output (or result). Here is a short example for a program that accepts a number from 1 to 100:

Type — Description · Example input · Expected output

Normal — Number from 1 to 100 allowed · 2 · Accepted

Normal — Number from 1 to 100 allowed · 99 · Accepted

Invalid — Number from 1 to 100 allowed · 0 · Not accepted

Invalid — Number from 1 to 100 allowed · 101 · Not accepted

Boundary — Number from 1 to 100 allowed · 1 · Accepted

concepts.title: Physical Computing with the micro:bit
concepts.explanation:
For this final subunit you will program a micro:bit, a small physical computer with a 5-by-5 grid of red LEDs, two buttons (A and B), motion sensors and a built-in radio. You will write MicroPython (a version of Python for small devices) at python.microbit.org. The best part: the website has a built-in simulator, so you can write and run micro:bit programs for free with no hardware at all. If you do have real micro:bits, everything works there too.

In the simulator you can press the on-screen buttons A and B, shake or tilt the device, change the temperature and light level, and watch the LED display respond - all in your browser. The simulator also lets you see the radio messages your program sends. Radio truly comes alive between two micro:bits, so if you have a partner with a device you can send real signals across the room.

First programs in the simulator

Every micro:bit program starts by importing the microbit module. This program scrolls a greeting across the LEDs - run it in the simulator and watch:

MicroPython: scrolls the word Hello across the LED display

This one counts how many times you press button A and shows the total. while True: repeats forever, and button_a.was_pressed() is True once each time the button is pressed:

MicroPython: a button-press counter

Communicating: wired and wireless

Devices communicate in two main ways. Wired transmission sends data down a cable, like a printer plugged into a computer. Wireless transmission sends data through the air using radio waves, like phone-to-headphone Bluetooth. Both devices must be set up to communicate the same way. The micro:bit has a built-in radio transmitter and receiver, so one micro:bit can send data wirelessly to another.

Radio signals can be picked up by any nearby device set to receive them. To keep messages organised, micro:bits use a group ID (a number). A micro:bit only receives messages sent to its own group. So both your micro:bit and your partner's must be set to the same group, and you should choose a different group from other pairs nearby, or you will pick up each other's messages by mistake. In MicroPython you set this up once at the start:

MicroPython: turn the radio on and set the group to 1

The radio.send() function transmits a string to every micro:bit in the same group. This sender transmits a message when you press A and a different one when you press B:

Note that radio.send() only sends strings. To send a number, convert it first with str(), for example radio.send(str(10)).

The receiver uses radio.receive(), which returns the next incoming message as a string, or None if nothing has arrived. Here the receiver shows a heart or a happy face depending on the message - this is exactly the selection you learned in 1.2 and 1.4, now controlling real hardware:

MicroPython: receiver program that reacts to the message

If you only want to display whatever text arrives, check that a message actually came in first:

MicroPython: display any message that is received

You can send data on other events too, such as a shake, using the motion sensor. This program sends the word 'shaken' when the micro:bit is shaken, and also shows any message it receives:

MicroPython: send on shake, and display anything received
concepts.example: Any device that can read radio data could pick up an unencrypted wireless signal. That is why real systems encrypt their data, scrambling it so that only the intended device can make sense of it. To everyone else it just looks like jumbled characters.

esafety.title: Keep personal information private
esafety.text: Your full name, address, school, phone number, birthday and passwords are personal information. Never type them into a game, an app or a website, and never send them to someone you only know online.

esafety.title: Check before you trust
esafety.text: Anyone can put anything on the internet, so not everything you read is true. Check an important fact on a second, different website, and ask an adult you trust if you are not sure.

esafety.title: Tell someone if something worries you
esafety.text: If anything online upsets you, or someone asks you for personal information or to keep a secret, stop, leave the page and tell an adult you trust straight away. It is never your fault.

esafety.title: Respect other people's work
esafety.text: Pictures, music and writing belong to whoever made them. Use work that is free to use, and say where you got it. Your own work belongs to you — put your name on it.

rules.title: input() always returns a string. Use int() or float() before doing maths.
Pseudocode vs Python
rules.text: Pseudocode is a plan with no fixed syntax; use = for comparison and the arrow for assignment. Python is real code with exact syntax; use == for comparison and = for assignment, and always end an if line with a colon.

rules.title: Indentation
rules.text: In Python there is no ENDIF. The indentation (four spaces) is what tells Python which lines are inside the if, elif, else, while or function.

rules.title: Booleans and casting
rules.text: True and False have no quotation marks. Any non-empty string casts to True (even the word False), an empty string casts to False, 0 casts to False and any other number casts to True.

rules.title: Libraries
rules.text: Import a library at the top with import, then call a function as library.function(). math.floor rounds down, math.ceil rounds up, and random.randint(a, b) includes both end values.

rules.title: Testing
rules.text: Never trust one test. Use normal, invalid and boundary data. Boundary values, right on the edge, catch the most bugs.

rules.title: micro:bit radio
rules.text: Turn the radio on with radio.on(), set the same group on both devices with radio.config, send strings with radio.send, and receive with radio.receive. You can test it all free in the simulator.

terms: Algorithm
A set of ordered steps that are followed to solve a problem or complete a task.
Pseudocode
A way of planning a program that is halfway between everyday English and real code; it has no fixed syntax.
High-level language
A programming language, such as Python, designed to be easy for humans to read and write.
Variable
A named location in memory that stores one item of data, which can change while the program runs.
Assignment
Storing a value in a variable, shown by <- in pseudocode or = in Python.
Identifier
The name given to a variable, constant or sub-routine.
Selection
Choosing which code to run based on whether a condition is true or false.
Condition
A comparison test that gives a result of either true or false.
Conditional statement
Code that runs different actions depending on whether a condition is true or false (an IF statement).
Boolean operator
AND, OR or NOT - used to combine or reverse conditions.
Indentation
Spaces at the start of a line; in Python, indentation shows which code is inside a block.
Linear search
